chain.g: to distribute, to give, to take

ety.text: Anglo-Norman noumbrebor. Middle English nombre English number Inherited from Middle English number, nombre, numbre, noumbre, from Anglo-Norman noumbre, Old French nombre, from Latin numerus (“number”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *nem- (“to distribute, to give, to take”). Compare Saterland Frisian Nummer, Nuumer, West Frisian nûmer, Dutch nummer (“number”), German Nummer (“number”), Danish nummer (“number”), Swedish nummer (“number”), Icelandic númer (“number”). Displaced Middle English ȝetæl and rime; more at tell, tale and rhyme.
Equivalent to numb (verb) + -er

senses.d: Quantity of countable things.
ex: Any number of people can be reading from a given repository at a time.
There are, in addition to all the red socks, a number that don’t suit me either.

senses.d: An abstract entity used to describe quantity.
ex: Zero, one, −1, 2.5, and pi are all numbers.

senses.d: A numeral: a symbol for a non-negative integer.
ex: The number 8 is usually made with a single stroke.

senses.d: An element of one of several sets: natural numbers, integers, rational numbers, real numbers, complex numbers, and sometimes extensions such as hypercomplex numbers, etc.
ex: The equation e#123;i#92;pi#125;#43;1#61;0 includes the most important numbers: 1, 0, #92;pi, i, and e.

senses.d: Indicating the position of something in a list or sequence. Abbreviations: No or No., no or no. (in each case, sometimes written with a superscript "o", like Nº or №). The symbol "#" is also used in this manner.
ex: Horse number 5 won the race.

senses.d: A sequence of digits and letters used to register people, automobiles, and various other items.
ex: Her passport number is C01X864TN.
You can take the number 8 (bus) all the way to the airport.

senses.d: A telephone number.
ex: Let's give her a call. Do you have her number handy?
I'm definitely interested. Here's my number. Call me back anytime.

senses.d: Of a word or phrase, the state of being singular, dual or plural, shown by inflection.
ex: Adjectives and nouns should agree in gender, number, and case.

senses.d: Poetic metres; verses, rhymes.
ex: Griefe brought to numbers cannot be ſo fierce, / For, he tames it, that fetters it in verſe.
As yet a Child, nor yet a Fool to Fame, / I liſp'd in Numbers, for the Numbers came.

senses.d: A performance; especially, a single song or song and dance routine within a larger show.
ex: For his second number, he sang "The Moon Shines Bright".

senses.d: To total or count; to amount to.
ex: I don’t know how many books are in the library, but they must number in the thousands.
Do they number in the hundreds, do they number in the thousands? Do they number in the tens of thousand?

senses.d: To limit to a certain number; to reckon (as by fate) to be few in number.
ex: The old man knew that his days were numbered.
THE DAYS OF ENGLAND NOT “NUMBERED.” REPLY TO SIR ARCHIBALD ALISON.

senses.d: To count; to determine the quantity of.
ex: The king ordered that all his subjects be numbered.
Who can number all the stars and who can count the desert sands?

senses.d: To label (items) with numbers; to assign numbers to (items).
ex: Number the baskets so that we can find them easily.

senses.d: To call out and assign a series of numbers (usually to people), either for the sake of dividing into groups or for counting.
ex: Shelley numbered off the group into two teams for the baseball game.
I counted them and numbered them off, and I found about three hundred and seventy or three hundred and seventy-five.

senses.d: To enumerate or list, especially while assigning numbers to.
To classify or include (in a group of things).
ex: Alexander the Great's army numbered an elite cavalry among its ranks.

senses.d: To be classified or included (in a certain group or category of things).
ex: Her horses number among the fastest in her country.
They number among our best people, particularly when we realise that they are models for what the rest of us might also achieve.

senses.d: Something that numbs.

grp.label: abstract entity used to describe quantity
used to show the rank of something in a list or sequence
grammar: state of being singular, dual or plural

ety.text: Inherited from Middle French nombre, from Old French nombre, nonbre, from Latin numerus. Doublet of numéro.
Borrowed from Latin numerus, whence also Italian novero (an inherited doublet).
Borrowed from Latin quantitātem, from quantus.
Borrowed from Latin numerus, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *nem- (“to assign, allot; take”).
Inherited from Old Spanish quantidat, borrowed from Latin quantitātem, from quantus (“how much”).

es:serie.gl: series (a number of things that follow one another)

ety.text: From Latin seriēs.
Borrowed from Latin quantitātem.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese número, from Latin numerus.
Borrowed from Italian numero. Doublet of nombre.
From Medieval Latin cifra (“zero”), from Andalusian Arabic صِفر (ṣifr, “empty”). Doublet of zéro.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin cifra (“zero, numeral”), from Arabic صِفْر (ṣifr, “zero, empty, nothing”). Doublet of zero.

chain.g: Of or belonging to a number; numeral.

ety.text: Latin numerālislbor. Portuguese numeral Learned borrowing from Latin numerālis.

phr: age ain't nothing but a number

ety.text: From the past participle of nim (“to take”). Compare German benommen (“dazed, numb”) and Old Norse numinn. The final ⟨b⟩ is a later addition; it was never pronounced, and did not appear in the original word.

senses.d: Physically unable to feel, not having the power of sensation.
ex: fingers numb with cold
legs numb from kneeling

senses.d: Emotionally unable to feel or respond in a normal way.
ex: numb with shock; numb with boredom
[…] seeing the dog—somehow that made me feel again. I’d been too dazed, too numb, to feel the full viciousness of it.

senses.d: Dumb or stupid.
Causing numbness.
ex:
[…] he did lap me
Even in his own garments, and gave himself,
All thin and naked to the numb cold night.

senses.d: To cause to become numb (physically or emotionally).
ex: The dentist gave me novocaine to numb my tooth before drilling, thank goodness.
When I first heard the news, I was numbed by the shock.

senses.d: To cause (a feeling) to be less intense.
ex: He turned to alcohol to numb his pain.
[I was] thankful for the pain, which helped to numb my terror.

senses.d: To cause (the mind, faculties, etc.) to be less acute.
ex: […] hunger, fatigue, and despairing hopelessness had numbed his brain […]

senses.d: To become numb (especially physically).
ex: […] after fumbling with numbing fingers for ten or fifteen minutes, he waved his hand with a gesture of despair […]

grp.label: to cause the mind or senses to be less acute

ety.text: Inherited from Old French [Term?], from Latin gurdus.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese dormente, from Latin dormientem, present active participle of dormiō (“to sleep”). By surface analysis, dormir + -ente.
From en- + gourd + -ir.
From en- + dormir or Latin indormīre.
From anesthésie + -er.
From in- + torpido (“torpid, sluggish”) + -ire.
From anestetico + -izzare.

chain.g: to fall asleep, go to sleep

ety.text: Inherited from Latin addormīscere. Compare Galician and Portuguese adormecer.

Borrowed from Latin intumēscere. According to Coromines & Pascual, first attested in Baltasar Gracián (17th century). The verb was partly affected by the inherited verb adormecer, producing some of the alternative forms shown above.
From Middle English numerous from Latin numerōsus (“numerous, abundant; harmonious”), from numerus (“number”). Doublet of numerose. Analyzeable as numero- + -ous.

senses.d: An indefinite large number of.
ex: There are numerous definitions of the word 'man'.
There are numerous reasons to refrain.

senses.d: Indefinitely large numerically; many.
ex: The reasons to refrain are numerous.

senses.d: Consisting of a large number of individuals or parts.
ex: A numerous band of men and maidens escorts him by torchlight.

senses.d: Having many different qualities.

ety.text: From nombre + -eux, or from Latin numerōsus.
Borrowed from Latin numerōsus. By surface analysis, numero + -oso. Compare novero.
Borrowed from Latin numerōsus; equivalent to número + -oso.
Borrowed from Latin numerōsus, from numerus (“number”), from Proto-Indo-European *nem- (“to assign, allot; take”). By surface analysis, número + -oso.
Latin -icuslbor. Old French -ique Middle French -ique French -ique French numériquebor. English numeric English -al English numerical From numeric + -al.

senses.d: Of or pertaining to numbers.
The same in number; hence, identically the same; identical.
ex: For who ever was yet seen by them, after a total consumption into dust and ashes, to rise again, and to resume the same numerical body?

ety.text: From Latin numerus (whence nombre) + -ique. Use in electronics is a semantic loan from English digital, which has also been directly borrowed into French.

pt:numérico.gl: numerical (of, pertaining to or using numbers)
